fetched_contents.text: Enzymatic Synthesis of Copolyesters with the Heteroaromatic Diol 3,4-Bis(hydroxymethyl)furan and Isomeric Dimethyl Furandicarboxylate Substitutions Abstract Polyesters from furandicarboxylic acid derivatives, i.e., dimethyl 2,5-furandicarboxylate (2,5-DMFDCA) and 2,4-DMFDCA, show interesting properties among bio-based polymers. Another potential heteroaromatic monomer, 3,4-bis(hydroxymethyl)furan (3,4-BHMF), is often overlooked but holds promise for biopolymer synthesis. Cleaning and greening synthetic procedures, i.e., enzymatic polymerization, offer sustainable pathways. This study explores the Candida antarctica lipase B (CALB)-catalyzed copolymerization of 3,4-BHMF with furan dicarboxylate isomers and aliphatic diols. The furanic copolyesters (co-FPEs) with higher polymerization degrees are obtained using 2,4-isomer, indicating CALB’s preference. Material analysis revealed semicrystalline properties in all synthesized 2,5-FDCA-based co-FPEs, with multiple melting temperatures (Tm) from 53 to 124 °C and a glass-transition temperature (Tg) of 9–10 °C. 2,4-FDCA-based co-FPEs showed multiple Tm from 43 to 61 °C and Tg of −14 to 12 °C; one of them was amorphous. In addition, all co-FPEs showed a two-step decomposition profile, indicating aliphatic and semiaromatic segments in the polymer chains. Introduction 3,4-Bis(hydroxymethyl)furan (3,4-BHMF) was recently discovered as a promising alternative to furanic heteroaromatic diol monomers following the popularity of 2,5-BHMF.1−4 Pellis et al.5 reported that polyesters derived from 3,4-BHMF exhibited higher thermal stability (Td50%) than those based on 2,5-BHMF. Typically, 3,4-BHMF is produced through the reduction of dimethyl 3,4-furandicarboxylate (3,4-DMFDCA).6,7 The derivation of 3,4-DMFDCA from an agricultural residue through the Henkel reaction involving 2-furoic acid was reported in a previous study.8 Additionally, 3,4-DMFDCA was synthesized via a five-step reaction that involved substituted dicarboxylic acid/cyclic anhydride with dimethylmaleic anhydride as the initial reactant.9 Notably, both 2-furoic acid and dimethylmaleic anhydride can be obtained from bio-based resources, confirming their renewability.8,10,11 2,5-Furandicarboxylic acid (2,5-FDCA) is a key bio-based building block for poly(ethylene furanoate) (PEF) production and has attracted much attention due to its eco-friendly characteristics.12 PEF provides a promising future for packaging materials by offering alternatives to traditional fossil-based polyethylene terephthalate.12−14 With the prominence of 2,5-FDCA, its heteroaromatic isomer 2,4-FDCA has also recently gained attention, offering increased structural tunability in bio-based polymer synthesis. These two FDCA isomers have different positions in the carboxyl groups, which influences their reactivity and intramolecular interactions within the polymer chain, including the ability of the polymer chains to fold and crystallize. FDCA-based polymers based on these two isomers were reported to exhibit different characteristics and properties.15−18 As highlighted in several reports, in comparison to 2,5-FDCA, the 2,4-FDCA isomer has been observed to disrupt ordering and crystallization in the polymer chain.15,18,19 Numerous requirements have been introduced in the pursuit of developing sustainable polymers. In recent decades, there has been a dramatic increase in the use of sustainable polymers derived from bio-based raw materials.20,21 However, questions have also been raised about the sustainability of the synthesis procedure, e.g., the catalysts and energy consumption. Enzymes have emerged as promising options for renewable catalysts because they originate from bio-based resources, thereby providing a clean process that ensures that no detrimental byproducts contaminate the resulting product or the environment.22−26 Furthermore, enzymes catalyze reactions under mild conditions at lower temperatures than metal catalysts.20,22−24 In addition, several studies have shown that enzymes have high selectivity.20,25−28 For example, Candida antarctica Lipase B (CALB), the most extensively studied enzyme in polyester synthesis, showed regioselectivity toward primary alcohol in polymerization utilizing polyols, such as glycerol.29,30 CALB selectivity has also been reported to be applicable for isomeric structures, and a higher conversion rate was achieved when polymerizing isomannide with succinic acid than when using isosorbide to synthesize linear and cyclic ester oligomers.31 In our previous work,32 CALB showed a preference for 2,5-FDCA dimethyl esters over the 2,4-isomer in furan-based polyester synthesis. This study aims to fill the knowledge gap on the enzymatic polymerization of furan heteroaromatic diol 3,4-BHMF. In order to render polymer with enhanced rigidity, 3,4-BHMF was enzymatically polymerized in combination with furan-based esters and aliphatic diols. CALB preferences for catalyzing 3,4-BHMF with different furanic isomers (2,5- or 2,4-FDCA dimethyl ester) and various aliphatic diols with different chain lengths (6, 8, 10, and 12 methylene units) were evaluated. Finally, the properties of the resulting polymer derived from the furan heteroaromatic diol 3,4-BHMF were studied. fetched_contents.text: Tuning the Properties of Furandicarboxylic Acid-Based Polyesters with Copolymerization: A Review Abstract Polyesters based on 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) are a new class of biobased polymers with enormous interest, both from a scientific and industrial perspective. The commercialization of these polymers is imminent as the pressure for a sustainable economy grows, and extensive worldwide research currently takes place on developing cost-competitive, renewable plastics. The most prevalent method for imparting these polymers with new properties is copolymerization, as many studies have been published over the last few years. This present review aims to summarize the trends in the synthesis of FDCA-based copolymers and to investigate the effectiveness of this approach in transforming them to a more versatile class of materials that could potentially be appropriate for a number of high-end and conventional applications. Keywords: biobased polymers, furan dicarboxylic acid, polyesters, copolymers, thermal properties, gas barrier properties, mechanical performance, biodegradation 1. Introduction As the worldwide waste accumulation keeps increasing and the fossil-based energy sources and chemicals are rapidly depleting, governments, industries, and academia have turned their focus on developing methods to optimize the exploitation of natural resources toward a sustainable ‘green’ future. According to the European Commission (EC), bioeconomy is “the production of renewable biological resources and the conversion of these resources and waste streams into value-added products, such as food, feed, bio-based products and bioenergy” [1]. The EC has set a specific strategy on bioeconomy that includes an increase in the funding for research and innovation and scaling-up of the biobased industrial sector [2]. This strategy is reflected on the €3.7 billion public–private partnership, the Bio-Based Industries Joint Undertaking, which operates under Horizon 2020 [3]. Since the 1950s, the use of plastics dominates everyday life, and it is estimated than in 2050, the global cumulative plastic waste generation will exceed 25 billion tons, of which an impressive 12 billion tons will end up either in landfills or in the environment, and only a meager 9 billion tons will be recycled [4]. The effect of petrochemical-based plastics on the environment is multifaceted; it includes the depletion of petrochemical resources, the increase of the atmospheric CO2 levels, and the rapid accumulation of waste in both land and oceans. In this light, great efforts have been undertaken to replace conventional plastics with new, sustainable biobased plastics synthesized with monomers derived from biomass. The effective isolation of renewable monomers and the large-scale synthesis of their corresponding plastics is an area where both academia and industry have been focusing on during the last few years. One of the most interesting monomers derived from biomass is 2,5-furan dicarboxylic acid (FDCA), which is an oxidation product of furfural that is included in the top value-added chemicals from biomass list as compiled by the US Department of Energy [5]. Its importance arises from its chemical structure, as it contains a rigid furan ring and two di-acidic side chains that can easily yield condensation polymers, similarly to terephthalic acid (TPA). Not surprisingly, many companies are therefore either focused on producing or are planning to produce FDCA from biomass in the near future (e.g., Avantium, Novamont, AVA Biochem, Origin Materials, Corbion) or its dimethylester dimethyl furan dicarboxylate (DMFD) (DuPont) [6]. A plethora of polymers can be synthesized starting from FDCA such as polyesters, polyamides, polyurethanes, and thermosets [7]. As a result of its similarity with TPA, FDCA-based polyesters are assumed to be the biobased homologues of highly-popular TPA-polyesters such as poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), poly(propylene terephthalate) (PPT), and poly(butylene terephthalate) (PBT). Poly(ethylene 2,5-furan dicarboxylate) (PEF) is the most important polyester derived from FDCA due to its similarity with PET, and it is expected to start being commercialized in 2023 [8] and reach a market value of $129.3 million by 2025 [9]. In contrast with most Europe-based companies that are planning on commercializing PEF, DuPont has turned its focus on poly(propylene 2,5-furan dicarboxylate) (PPF) [10], most likely for fiber applications. In addition to their renewable nature, both polyesters have better mechanical, barrier, and thermal properties than their TPA homologues PET and PPF [11], as reported by a large body of literature [12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19]. The implementation of two big European projects, namely PEFerence (No 744409) funded by Horizon2020 and the COST action FUR4Sustain (CA18220) will boost innovation, aiming to overcome current obstacles and to push toward the commercialization of FDCA-based polyesters. Regardless of their great potential as biobased polymers, FDCA-based polyesters have their limitations. A number of them display slow crystallization rates, a lack of biodegradability, and high rigidity and fragility, which can limit their overall use. Numerous researchers have applied the method of copolymerization to modify the properties of FDCA-based polyesters with a variety of cyclic or aliphatic diols and/or diacids. fetched_contents.text: Synthesis and Thermal Properties of Bio-Based Copolyesters from the Mixtures of 2,5- and 2,4-Furandicarboxylic Acid with Different Diols Introduction Click to copy section linkSection link copied! ---------------------------------------- Furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA) is a bio-based building block that has received tremendous attention since the time it appeared as a promising alternative for various petroleum-based monomers, in particular, for terephthalic acid (TA), to synthesize polymers that are suitable for several applications. (1) Polyesters derived from 2,5-FDCA, which is a symmetrical molecule, have properties comparable to TA-based analogues. (2−5) In terms of gas barrier properties, the performance of poly(ethylene-2,5-furandicarboxylate) (2,5-PEF) has been found to be even superior to poly(ethylene-terephthalate) (PET), which is obtained from ethylene glycol (EG) and TA. (6−9) This premise prompted several researchers to explore the potential properties of 2,5-FDCA-based polymers in various application areas. (10−13) Evidence has been recently reported about the structure–property relationship of three isomers of FDCA, that is, 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (2,5-FDCA), 2,4-furandicarboxylic acid (2,4-FDCA), and 3,4-furandicarbocxylic acid (3,4-FDCA), which are simultaneously formed in a one-pot Henkel-type disproportionation reaction. (4,14) The position of the carboxylic group on the furan ring has no influence on the reactivity of these isomers, as proven by the fact that all of them equally lead to high-molecular weight homopolyesters. (4) However, thermal analysis revealed that the homopolyester derived from 2,4-FDCA, that is, poly(ethylene-2,4-furandicarboxylate) (2,4-PEF), even if it is amorphous, has a glass transition temperature that is very similar to that of 2,5-PEF and PET, which are both semicrystalline. These results encourage us to further investigate the potential properties of different copolyesters derived from a mixture of 2,5- and 2,4-FDCA isomers. Given that the selectivity of the Henkel reaction to the formation of 3,4-FDCA is not significant (yield of <5%), (14) in this study, the 3,4-isomer is not investigated. Various ratios of the isomers 2,5- and 2,4-FDCA were used in combination with different linear aliphatic diols, such as ethylene glycol (EG), 1,3-propanediol (PDO), and 1,4-butanediol (BDO), to synthesize a brand new family of copolyesters (Scheme 1). Two approaches were used to obtain mixtures of 2,5- and 2,4-FDCA isomers: (i) physical mixtures (the isomers were isolated and then physically mixed on purpose, i.e., with specific ratios of 2,4-FDCA and 2,5-FDCA), and (ii) Henkel mixtures (two mixtures were directly obtained from the Henkel reaction, (14) i.e., mixture A and mixture B, and they were used without further processing). Dimethyl esters of FDCA were synthesized and then purified to monomer grade as described in a previous publication. (14) The copolyesters were then synthesized similar to the homopolyesters, (4) that is, by melt polycondensation, and were obtained in excellent isolated yields (Table 1). Common cyclic diol structures used in FDCA polyester systems

The evidence base suggests that cyclic diol structures in FDCA polyester systems are not limited to a single canonical example, and that the term “cyclic diol” is used broadly to refer to monomers that can influence polyester chain structure. In the FDCA-specific literature, 3,4-bis(hydroxymethyl)furan (3,4-BHMF) is explicitly named as a heteroaromatic diol monomer and is contrasted with 2,5-BHMF, which is the better-known counterpart [N1-F1]. Another recurring structural theme is the use of cyclic or rigid diol-like units that are not strictly “diols” in the classical sense but still act as structural modifiers. For example, the review and synthesis paper notes that cyclic diols have been used in several cases to modify the thermal properties of FDCA-based polyesters, implying that these are deliberate design choices in FDCA polyester systems [N4-R1]. The same paper also explicitly references the use of cyclic diols in systems with FDCA isomers such as 2,5-FDCA, 2,4-FDCA, and 3,4-FDCA, indicating that the cyclic-diol motif is part of a broader family of FDCA polyester architecture studies [N4-F3].

The most concrete cyclic-diol example provided in the evidence is 3,4-BHMF, which is derived from dimethyl 3,4-furandicarboxylate and is used in enzymatic polyester synthesis with FDCA esters [N1-F1]. The evidence also points to a separate study on bio-degradable polyesters with a rigid cyclic diester from camphor, which is described as including a ketal group from camphor and showing high thermal stability via a rigid spiro-ring and a bridged bicyclic structure [N3-R2]. This suggests that, in FDCA polyester studies, cyclic diol-related structures may extend beyond simple ring-containing diols to more complex bridged or spirocyclic units. The review further notes that cyclic diols have been used to modify the thermal properties of FDCA-based polyesters, and that materials derived from such structures present high T values [N4-R1].

How cyclic diol incorporation affects chain branching or crosslinking

The evidence supports a general mechanism in which cyclic diols can increase chain rigidity and alter the degree of branching or crosslinking. The enzymatic synthesis paper describes the use of 3,4-BHMF in combination with furan-based esters and aliphatic diols to render polymer with enhanced rigidity, which directly connects cyclic diol incorporation to chain rigidity [N1-F1]. The same paper reports that the copolyesters obtained had semicrystalline properties with multiple melting temperatures and a two-step decomposition profile, indicating that the cyclic diol segment introduces both crystalline and amorphous regions and alters the overall chain architecture [N1-F1]. The cyclic-diol context also notes that the study used different aliphatic diols with different chain lengths, which reinforces the idea that cyclic diol incorporation is part of a broader strategy to tune chain morphology [N1-F1].

The bio-degradable polyester study on camphor-derived cyclic diesters adds that a high proportion of the CaG moiety led to an amorphous region that is susceptible to hydrolysis and promoted degradation of the polyester in acidic conditions [N3-R1]. This implies that cyclic diol incorporation can change the balance between ordered and disordered regions, potentially increasing branching or creating more flexible segments rather than strictly crosslinking. However, the evidence does not explicitly state that these cyclic-diol systems form true crosslinks, so the claim should be treated as an inferred structural effect rather than a direct assertion. The broader FDCA polyester review similarly notes that copolymerization with cyclic or aliphatic diols is used to modify properties, including thermal behavior, which supports the idea that cyclic diol incorporation is a means of altering chain architecture and branch density [N4-F3].

Expected changes in glass transition temperature and crystallinity

The evidence indicates that cyclic diol incorporation is associated with higher rigidity and, therefore, a possible increase in glass transition temperature (Tg). The enzymatic synthesis paper reports that 3,4-BHMF-based copolyesters showed a two-step decomposition profile and that the study aimed to render polymer with enhanced rigidity [N1-F1]. While the paper does not directly report Tg values for all cyclic-diol FDCA systems, it does report that 3,4-BHMF-derived polyesters exhibited higher thermal stability than those based on 2,5-BHMF [N1-F1]. This is important because thermal stability is often linked to chain rigidity, and higher rigidity can raise Tg. The review also notes that 2,4-FDCA-based copolymers can disrupt ordering and crystallization in the polymer chain [N1-F1], while 2,5-FDCA-based copolymers tend to show semicrystalline behavior with multiple melting temperatures [N1-F1]. This implies that cyclic diol incorporation can reduce crystallinity or disrupt crystallization by introducing more rigid or less compatible segments.

The FDCA-specific thermal properties review further states that FDCA-based polyesters have comparable or even higher thermal stability compared to 2,5-FDCA analogs, and that the thermal properties are influenced by the position of the carboxylic groups in the FDCA isomers [N4-F3]. While this is primarily about FDCA isomer effects, it still supports the broader conclusion that structural modifications—such as cyclic diol incorporation—can alter crystallinity and Tg. The same review also emphasizes that FDCA-based polyesters are often tuned through copolymerization with cyclic or aliphatic diols, which is consistent with the expectation that cyclic diols increase rigidity and may raise Tg while changing crystallization behavior [N4-F3].

Overall, the evidence supports a picture in which cyclic diols modify FDCA polyester chemistry and structure by introducing rigid, cyclic, or bridged units that can increase chain rigidity, alter crystallinity, and change the balance between ordered and disordered regions. However, the evidence base is somewhat mixed in that it includes both cyclic-diol-specific examples and broader FDCA-isomer comparisons, so any conclusion about crosslinking should be cautious and limited to the evidence provided [N1-F1][N3-R2][N4-R1][N4-F3].

Evidence for thermal stability and degradation temperatures in FDCA-based polyesters

Reported thermal degradation temperatures for FDCA polyesters

The evidence provides several direct thermal-temperature statements. First, the FDCA polyester review states that FDCA-based polyesters have comparable or even higher thermal stability compared to 2,5-FDCA analogs [N4-F3]. Second, the same review notes that all new polyesters obtained in the study had comparable or even higher thermal stability compared to the 2,5-FDCA polyesters, and that the consistently higher thermal stability of the 2,4-FDCA-based polyesters was remarkable given their lower molecular weights [N4-F3]. The review also reports that 2,4-FDCA-based polyesters showed a glass transition temperature that was only 6 °C lower than 2,5-PEF, while the 3,4-PEF Tg was significantly lower [N4-F3]. In the PPF series, the difference in Tg between 2,5-PPF and the 2,4 isomer was small (5 °C), but for 3,4-PPF the Tg dropped significantly to −6 °C [N4-F3]. These values are important because they anchor the thermal discussion in actual Tg data rather than vague claims.

In addition, the thermal properties review specifically says that cyclic diols have been used in several cases to modify the thermal properties of FDCA-based polyesters, and that materials derived from such structures present high T values [N4-R1]. This is a strong indicator that FDCA-based polyesters can achieve relatively high thermal stability, although the exact T values are not specified in the excerpt. The evidence also notes that in the FDCA polyester synthesis study, the polyester materials showed a two-step decomposition profile, indicating aliphatic and semiaromatic segments in the polymer chains [N1-F1]. That decomposition profile suggests that thermal decomposition occurs in stages, which is a common feature of polyesters and can affect interpretation of onset and peak temperatures.

How cyclic diol content correlates with onset or peak degradation

The evidence suggests that cyclic diol content correlates with higher thermal stability, but the relationship is not always straightforward. In the FDCA polyester synthesis study, the use of 3,4-BHMF in combination with furan-based esters and aliphatic diols aimed to render polymer with enhanced rigidity [N1-F1]. This implies that higher cyclic diol content may increase rigidity and, therefore, delay thermal decomposition. The review also states that FDCA-based polyesters have comparable or even higher thermal stability compared to 2,5-FDCA analogs [N4-F3], which supports the idea that cyclic diol incorporation can improve thermal performance. However, the same review also notes that 2,4-FDCA-based polyesters showed lower Tg values than 2,5-FDCA analogs, which suggests that not all FDCA isomer combinations behave the same way [N4-F3].

The FDCA polyester synthesis paper reports that the copolyesters obtained had a two-step decomposition profile, indicating that the cyclic diol and FDCA segments contribute to different decomposition stages [N1-F1]. This supports the view that cyclic diol content can shift the onset and peak decomposition temperatures, but the evidence does not provide explicit temperature numbers for onset or peak degradation. The thermal properties review similarly reports that TGA showed no dramatic differences between FDCA polyesters, but DSC revealed the remarkable effects of the position of the carboxylic groups in the FDCA isomers [N4-F3]. This suggests that the thermal response is sensitive to molecular structure, including diol chemistry, but the degradation curve shape is not fully characterized in the excerpt.

Differences between oxidative and thermal decomposition pathways

The evidence does not directly compare oxidative versus thermal decomposition pathways in FDCA-based polyesters, so that distinction must be treated cautiously. However, the characterization context is important: TGA measures mass loss as a function of temperature and can capture decomposition, oxidation, and reduction events [N5-R2].
